claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1, 2, 3, and 7, run a realistic sequential-edit benchmark comparing parameter-based editors (ROME, MEMIT if available, MEND, KE, constrained fine-tuning) against parameter-free or parameter-preserving methods (IKE and, if implementation permits, a retrieval/memory editor such as SERAC/T-Patcher) on GPT-2 and GPT-J using public COUNTERFACT and ZSRE splits. Filter out unrecallable/trivial instances as the field expects, then apply edits cumulatively with no rollback at batch sizes 1, 10, 100, and 1000, measuring Reliability/ES on edited prompts, Generalization/PS on paraphrases and equivalence neighborhoods, Locality/NS on out-of-scope prompts, plus downstream robustness on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions before and after each cumulative edit block. Include the unedited model, in-context editing baseline, and standard fine-tuning controls. If near-perfect single-edit reports collapse under cumulative edits or if robustness tasks degrade as edit count rises, that supports the claim that parameter editing is not reliably updating facts without harming core capabilities and that damage compounds. If parameter editors retain high Reliability, Generalization, Locality, and downstream performance even after many sequential edits, the central claim is weakened. This experiment becomes less necessary if there already exists a public, cross-method, no-rollback benchmark covering these models, datasets, and downstream tasks under identical preprocessing and filters.

To address subclaim 4, 5, and 6, perform a geometry-and-propagation study around actual weight edits. For each successful and unsuccessful edit from ROME/MEND/KE on GPT-2 and GPT-J, capture hidden-state representations for subject tokens across large public text samples and COUNTERFACT/ZSRE prompts, estimate each edited layer’s covariance spectrum, and decompose the induced activation change Delta h caused by the local weight update into principal directions of the pre-edit representation space. Quantify whether edit-induced changes have disproportionately large projection or downstream logit impact along low-variance eigen-directions, then trace propagation by measuring activation differences layer-by-layer and token-by-token on both edited prompts and unrelated prompts. Replicate localization with both causal tracing and representation zeroing, and run layer/token sweeps to ensure the result is not a tracing artifact. If low-variance directions consistently show larger amplification and those perturbations spread to unrelated contexts across later layers, that supports a geometric and global-propagation explanation. If amplification is isotropic or confined to edited contexts, the geometric thesis is weakened and incidental implementation details become more plausible. This experiment could be partly obviated by prior public analyses that already publish eigenspace decompositions and propagation maps across multiple editors and backbones under matched settings.

To address subclaim 2 and to discriminate against the rival explanation that apparent locality merely reflects metric artifacts, evaluate broad capability preservation after editing. Starting from the same edited checkpoints produced in experiment 1, measure not only Locality on out-of-scope COUNTERFACT/ZSRE neighborhoods but also perplexity on held-out public text, next-token accuracy on LAMBADA, multiple-choice accuracy on HellaSwag, QA performance on Natural Questions, and consistency/fluency indicators such as average output length stability and self-agreement across paraphrases. Compare parameter editors, constrained fine-tuning, in-context editing, and parameter-free memory-style methods. The key analysis is whether methods that score well on standard edit metrics still show collateral drops on unrelated capabilities, especially as sequential edits accumulate. If broad-task performance declines while standard locality remains superficially acceptable, that supports the claim that parameter editing damages core capabilities and that conventional evaluation is too optimistic. If unrelated-task performance is stable, the damage claim is narrowed to benchmark-local effects. This experiment is less necessary if standard edit benchmarks are extended to include widely accepted public robustness suites and those results are already available for cumulative edits.

To address subclaim 3 specifically, replicate prior near-perfect editing claims under both canonical and realistic evaluation settings. Reproduce the reported single-edit, rollback-based results for at least one leading parameter editor on COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, then systematically add the controls the field expects: paraphrase/equivalence neighborhoods, portability-style probes where possible, out-of-scope locality sets, alternative dataset replication, layer/location sweeps, corruption-magnitude sensitivity for causal tracing-linked methods, and most importantly sequential no-rollback evaluation. Also compare with an in-context editing baseline and a parameter-preserving editor under the same prompts. If performance is near-perfect only on canonical prompts with rollback and falls substantially on paraphrases, neighborhoods, cross-dataset tests, or cumulative settings, that directly supports the claim that earlier near-perfect results do not survive realistic evaluation. If the near-perfect results remain robust across these stricter settings, that undermines a major pillar of the claim. This experiment could be unnecessary if a trusted third-party reproduction already exists that extends the exact published protocols with these realistic controls.

To address subclaim 8, 9, and 10, test whether a parameter-free approach is a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback by comparing edit quality, persistence, scalability, and side effects under equal resource budgets. Use IKE and, if available, a public parameter-preserving memory editor versus ROME/MEND/KE on GPT-2 and GPT-J over COUNTERFACT and ZSRE. Verify weight immutability by hashing model parameters before and after inference-time editing or memory attachment; separately count any extra parameters or memory footprint. Measure Reliability, Generalization, Locality, and runtime/latency as edit count grows, plus robustness-task preservation from HellaSwag/LAMBADA/Natural Questions. The critical question is not whether parameter-free methods win every metric, but whether they offer comparable edit success with better locality/capability preservation and practical scaling, which would make them serious alternatives. If parameter-free methods are clearly inferior on edit success while offering little stability benefit, they look more like fallbacks; if they match or approach success while preserving capabilities and avoiding cumulative damage, the claim is strengthened. This experiment would be partly unnecessary if there were already standardized head-to-head evaluations of parameter-changing and parameter-free editors under matched prompts, compute, and sequential-edit settings.

With respect to evidence piece 'Layer and token sweep' and the rival explanation that edit-layer choice drives observed effects, run a controlled regression-style intervention study. For each fact to edit, apply the same parameter-editing algorithm across many candidate layers and subject-token positions, including layers suggested by causal tracing and layers chosen uniformly at random. Record edit success, generalization, locality, and downstream capability change, then fit models predicting outcomes from layer identity alone, tracing-derived importance alone, and both together. Repeat with alternative localization via representation zeroing and with multiple corruption magnitudes where tracing is used. If layer identity explains most variance and localization adds little once layer is controlled, then some geometric/localization claims may be overstated or confounded by where edits happen. If localization-derived scores predict success and collateral damage beyond layer choice, that strengthens the mechanistic account and helps target where harmful global propagation originates. This experiment becomes less necessary if published multi-backbone layer-sweep datasets already expose per-layer edit outcomes and localization scores for the same edit instances.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 includes an unedited model and a no-rollback cumulative schedule whose first condition is a single edit, while experiment 3 explicitly contrasts canonical and realistic evaluation and reproduces single-edit results. Together they provide both the baseline and the realistic inference comparison.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Independent validation that semantic judgments of edit quality agree with a deterministic token-level measure across the same reliability, generalization, locality, and portability outcomes.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set collects standard edit scores, broad capability scores, fluency indicators, and several alternative evaluation conditions, so it does measure the relevant outcomes in more than one way. However, it does not require the same generations to be scored by both an independent semantic evaluator and a deterministic token-level measure, leaving evaluator-dependent ranking artifacts unresolved.

The proposed experiments report standard edit metrics and downstream-task outcomes but do not mandate a semantic-versus-deterministic cross-check on identical outputs.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A normalized, direction-specific measurement of representation change that identifies amplification in low-variance directions and tests whether the affected-direction fraction increases with cumulative edit count across editing methods and model architectures.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 directly measures covariance spectra, principal-direction projections, downstream impact, and layer/token propagation, while experiment 5 adds localization and layer controls and experiment 0 supplies cumulative edits. But the geometry study is not explicitly run across cumulative edit counts, does not state the relative normalization or threshold needed to test an R_k-like amplification criterion, and is limited to two backbones and three named editors. Thus it can reveal low-variance directional effects and propagation, but the accumulation-dependent mechanism remains ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference requires more than observing projections: it tests normalized amplification relative to singular values and its monotonic growth as edits accumulate.
[2] Proposed experiment 1 measures projections and low-variance effects, and proposed experiment 0 creates cumulative edited checkpoints.
[3] The proposals do not explicitly connect the directional analysis to each cumulative edit count or define a normalized threshold/fraction whose monotonic trend would be tested.

[4] A team could therefore find low-variance amplification without knowing whether it grows with edit accumulation in the claimed manner, and would fail to learn the full causal mechanism established by the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A multi-method, multi-condition sequential benchmark that compares representative parameter-changing and parameter-free approaches on factual-edit success and collateral-edit dimensions over increasing edit counts and more than one language-model setting.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed union performs no-rollback cumulative evaluation at 1, 10, 100, and 1000 edits, includes several distinct parameter-editing families and parameter-free or parameter-preserving controls, uses factual-edit datasets and multiple model backbones, and reports edit quality, locality, portability-style/generalization measures, and downstream preservation. The particular reference methods, datasets, model sizes, and full-dataset endpoint are not binding to the claim. This would establish whether representative parameter editors degrade under realistic accumulation and whether a parameter-free competitor remains viable.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evaluation of unrelated reasoning and broad language-model capabilities on edited checkpoints after fixed cumulative edit loads, allowing collateral damage to be separated from mere failure to edit the target facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiments 0 and 2 explicitly measure held-out text perplexity, next-token prediction, commonsense choice, question answering, fluency and consistency before and after cumulative edits, with attention to degradation as edit count rises. These are independent downstream capabilities and therefore address whether editing damages core behavior rather than merely lowering edit-locality scores. The reference's particular mathematics and general benchmarks are not required by the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A robustness sweep over model scale, knowledge representation or event type, fact difficulty, and editor configuration or architecture, showing whether the observed collapse is general or confined to a particular regime or implementation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set does test some robustness dimensions: it compares multiple editors, datasets, GPT-2 and GPT-J backbones, layers, subject-token positions, localization procedures, and tracing corruption magnitudes. Those controls could reveal dependence on editor placement, tracing, or particular small-model settings. However, it omits larger model scales, event-level knowledge, confidence-stratified fact difficulty, and the specific hyperparameter/architecture sensitivity of the method that does not collapse. The generality boundary therefore remains unresolved.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference asks whether the result persists across scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and editor configuration rather than being an artifact of one regime.
[2] Proposed experiments 0-5 cover some editor, backbone, layer, token, localization, corruption, and dataset variation.

[4] The team would learn that some implementation and localization variations were tested, but would fail to learn whether the collapse is general across scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and the key editor configuration boundaries.

The cumulative benchmark in proposed experiment 0 records edit quality and downstream robustness, but not the directional representation statistic needed to connect accumulation to low-variance amplification.

Thus the set could show a geometric effect for isolated edits but would not establish whether that effect compounds monotonically with sequential editing; the team would fail to learn the full cumulative mechanism.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A common sequential benchmark comparing parameter-changing and weight-preserving editing approaches across multiple edit counts, knowledge settings, model families, and the four dimensions of edit quality, with a criterion for cumulative collapse versus preservation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 supplies a sequential, no-rollback comparison at edit counts 1, 10, 100, and 1000 on two knowledge benchmarks, with multiple parameter-based and parameter-free methods and reliability, generalization, and locality measures. Experiment 4 adds a matched head-to-head comparison and checks persistence, side effects, and weight preservation. The particular models, method count, and benchmark names in the reference are not binding on the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Independent evaluations of untargeted reasoning and broad knowledge capabilities before and after fixed cumulative edit counts, allowing collateral capability damage to be distinguished from failure to edit the target facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and Natural Questions before and after each cumulative edit block, including 10 and 100 edits. Experiment 2 broadens this with held-out-text perplexity, next-token accuracy, multiple-choice performance, and QA, all on unrelated capabilities. These are independent capability checks rather than merely edit-benchmark locality scores, so different task choices do not prevent learning whether collateral damage occurs.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Cross-scope stress testing over model scale, fact representation and difficulty, and editor configuration, sufficient to distinguish a general limitation from an artifact of one model size, knowledge type, fact subset, or implementation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set varies editors, uses two knowledge benchmarks, and performs layer, token-position, localization, and corruption-magnitude sweeps. Those tests address some implementation and dataset dependence. It does not test larger model scales, event-level knowledge, high- versus low-confidence facts, or the broader architecture and hyperparameter sensitivity needed to rule out the main scope confounds.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment tests whether the observed collapse survives changes in model scale, fact representation, fact difficulty, and editor configuration.
Proposed experiments 0 and 3 vary methods, edit counts, and benchmark datasets, while experiment 5 varies layers, token positions, localization choices, and corruption magnitudes.

No proposed experiment varies scale upward, event-level versus triple-shaped knowledge, confidence-defined fact difficulty, or the full architecture and hyperparameter conditions identified as possible exceptions.
Therefore the proposed results could still be specific to the tested scale or fact distribution; the team would fail to learn whether the limitation is general rather than setup-specific.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would provide substantial evidence for realistic sequential degradation, collateral capability loss, global propagation, and the practical viability of a weight-preserving alternative. It would not, however, settle the claim as written: the scoring instrument is not directly validated against deterministic correctness, the geometric amplification mechanism is not tracked as a directional quantity over cumulative edits, and important scale, knowledge-type, and difficulty alternatives remain open.
missing: A same-output cross-check between semantic evaluation and deterministic token-level correctness across all edit dimensions.
Directional amplification measurements at successive cumulative edit counts, with an explicit monotonicity test across methods and architectures.
Stress tests over larger model scales, event-level knowledge, fact difficulty/confidence, and the relevant architecture and hyperparameter regimes.
